text.p: The following are the main stories from Wednesday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG

- German Finance Minister Theo Waigel and Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer set aside a dispute over the revaluation of gold and currency reserves with a deal that would see profits from such a move paid out to state finances only from 1998, as opposed to this year, as the government wanted.

- French election-winners negotiate over the formation of the new government after the 15-minute signing-in of new prime minister Lionel Jospin. Jospin holds meetings with members of the French Communists, who will be seeking appointments in return for support of the government.
- Newly-reelected Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien makes a plea for unity to the country.
BUSINESS
- World Bank ready to provide Russia with credit guarantees worth some 1.7 billion dollars.

- Germany's main banking sector federation says European monetary union must start as planned in 1999 and says the Maastricht Treaty on EMU nowhere states that the tough deficit-to-GDP criterion must be met precisely.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG

- Bonn not to use windfall from gold revaluation until 1998. Finance Minister Waigel has backed down in the row with the Bundesbank over use of its gold and currency reserves and has agreed not to use profits from any revaluation of these reserves this year, the period which determines qualification for EMU in 1999.
- Germany is looking increasingly isolated in its continued opposition to proposals for a European-wide initiative on jobs creation in the unemployment-hit continent.
- Sweden says it will not enter EMU on the planned start-date of 1999, calling the project "very uncertain".
HANDELSBLATT
- Bonn and Bundesbank set aside row over gold reserves, with government agreeing to delay implementation of profits from any such move.
- Trade union leaders in the west German chemical sector have for the first time agreed to allow employers there room to set pay deals independently of collective bargaining process.
- German authorities impose a record 265 million-mark fine on the ringleaders of a long-standing cartel in the heavy-duty electricity cable market.
DIE WELT

- Chancellor Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) and sister party the Christian Social Union (CSU) threaten junior government partners the Free Democrats (FDP) with reforming the current coalition into a "grand coalition" comprising other major parties. Such a move would mean the FDP, which is at odds with its government partners on tax and budget issues, would lose influence.
- Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien and his Liberal Party manage to scrape an absolute majority in parliamentary elections.
- Pope John Paul urges European governments to resist any moves that would threaten the building of a united Europe.
- A top U.S. lawyer who charges $485 an hour has been sought to extract U.S. Bill Clinton from the Paula Jones affair.
BUSINESS

- Building giants Hochtief and Holzmann, together with the Deutsche Bank, call off a plan that would have meant greater cooperation between the two after they learn the deal would be vetted by German cartel authorities.
